newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Profiles of major players in PNG political crisis.
newsitem.headline: Profiles of major players in PNG political crisis.

text.p: Papua New Guinea's latest political crisis pits a wily prime minister and urbane political survivor against a soft-spoken "soldier's soldier" who has become an unlikely focus of dissent.
Here are brief portraits of the two men:
Chan, 55, is serving his second term as prime minister and is a major figure in the South Pacific country's transition from an Australian territory since independence was granted in 1975.
Prime minister from 1980-82, he has spent 24 years in the Papua New Guinea parliament, the last five pushing the exploitation of the nation's vast natural resources.
His decision to hire foreign mercenaries to end a rebellion on copper-rich Bougainville island led to the current crisis.
Educated in Australia and first elected to parliament in 1968, he was finance minister from 1972-77, and held top posts with the International Monetary Fund, World Bank and Asian Development Bank.
Chan toppled elected leader Sir Michael Somare in a no-confidence vote in 1982. Somare beat him in a subsequent general election.
Chan was sworn in again in August 1994 after a long-running feud with prime minister Paias Wingti and stints in finance and foreign affairs posts.

Singirok, 40, was chosen by Chan in November 1995 to head the Papua New Guinea Defence Force (PNGDF) over a number of more senior officers, mainly because he shared the view that there could be no military solution to the Bougainville rebellion.
Singirok was sacked after calling for Chan to resign on Monday over the decision to hire mercenaries to fight on Bougainville.

He served three tours on Bougainville, two as a lieutenant-colonel in command and one as head of military intelligence, winning praise at home and on Bougainville after being wounded trying to rescue a fallen comrade.
Singirok attempted to rebuild relations between Port Moresby and local communities on Bougainville.
He has risen rapidly through the ranks in his 20-year military career, which has included several stints at military schools in Australia as student and tutor.
